reels.caption:
WHODUNIT #01 · An animated limestone wall full of finger pockets, and three suspects for who made them.

The culprit is rain. Rainwater picks up CO₂ from the air, and far more from the soil it seeps through, and becomes a weak acid. Over thousands of years it dissolves limestone and attacks the weakest spots first: fossils, burrows, fine cracks. (Not every pocket forms this way.)

Send this to the friend who lives for pocket routes.

reels.caption:
HOLD ID #01 · An animated climber hangs on a pale stripe in a rock wall, then we cut the rock open to show how the stripe formed and why it sticks out as an edge.

It started as a crack. Hot water moving through the crust carried dissolved silica; when it cooled or the pressure dropped, quartz crystallised on the crack walls and grew inward until the crack was sealed. Much later, at the surface, the vein can outlast the rock around it: quartz is one of the minerals most resistant to chemical weathering. Not every vein sticks out, and a fractured one can come off as a plate, so test it like any other hold.

Send this to the friend who always goes straight for the white edge.

reels.caption:
MYTH OR ROCK #01 · Sandstone after rain: when can you climb again? An animated climber on a sandstone boulder drying in the sun after rain, and what happens when they pull on the sloper.

Fontainebleau sandstone wears a thin, hard silica crust over much softer sand. After rain the surface dries first, while the sand underneath can stay damp, and wet sandstone can lose a lot of its strength: the water cancels the capillary tension between the grains and weakens the rock at the tips of tiny cracks. The crust forms only slowly, so a broken hold never grows back. How long to wait depends on sun, wind and humidity: after a soaking give it a day or two, longer when it's cool and damp.

Send this to the friend who says "it's basically dry" after every shower.

reels.caption:
REWIND #01 · What was the limestone of Germany's highest peak once? An animated climber on the Zugspitze summit wall, then 235 million years in rewind: the mountain sinks, the sea comes back and a reef grows.

The Zugspitze is built of Wetterstein limestone, the first big carbonate platform of the Northern Calcareous Alps and more than 1,400 m thick there. It formed in the warm Tethys sea about 235–240 million years ago: corals, calcareous sponges and algae built reefs at the platform's rim, with a shallow lagoon behind them, so "reef" is a slight simplification for the whole wall. Alpine mountain building later stacked and lifted these rocks into today's summit.

Send this to your climbing partner who has the Zugspitze on their list.

reels.caption:
HOLD ID #02 · An animated climber pinches a tufa on a limestone wall, then we zoom into its tip and watch how this hold forms.

Tufas aren't carved out of the wall, they grow onto it. Water that has dissolved limestone seeps out of the rock; once it loses CO₂, it is oversaturated and calcite comes out of solution, layer by layer, the way a stalactite grows after countless drops. That makes a tufa younger than the wall it hangs on. (Mosses and algae can help along, and most tufas on climbing walls have never been dated.)

Send this to the friend who plans every climbing trip around tufas.

reels.caption:
SCALE JUMP #01 · What is a chalk hold made of? An animated climber on a chalk wall, then we zoom from the hold into a sugar-cube-sized sample and on into the tiny plates it is built from.

The plates are coccoliths: calcite armour of single-celled algae, mostly 4–12 micrometres across. When the algae die, the plates sink and pile up on the sea floor, and over time that ooze hardens into chalk. In Cretaceous chalk from Kansas, Hattin and Darko counted between half a billion and six billion coccoliths in a single cubic centimetre. But intact plates fill only about a fifth of the rock at most (their own estimate, which they called tentative): much of the rest is plates that have already fallen apart, plus foraminifera, shell fragments, fish bones and mud. (And the chalk in your bag is something else: climbing chalk is magnesium carbonate.)

Send this to your climbing partner who always wants to know what the rock is made of.

reels.caption:
MYTH OR ROCK #02 · Climbers say the Frankenjura is limestone. An animated climber on a pocketed tower next to a bedded wall, then we scan both rocks and zoom into the crystal lattice.

It depends: the crags of the Franconian Jura are reef dolomites and massive limestones, both from a tropical Jurassic sea about 150 million years ago. Dolomite started out as limestone; later, magnesium replaced part of the calcium, and in the mineral dolomite, CaMg(CO₃)₂, every second calcium site holds magnesium. (The lattice in the reel is a sketch, not to scale, and the tower is one drawn example, not a rule for every crag.)

Send this to the friend who calls every Frankenjura crag perfect limestone.

reels.thema: Gradierte Schichtung: Which way was up?
reels.caption:
WHODUNIT #02 · Which way was up on a sandstone crag? An animated climber brushes a bedded wall and finds the coarse grains at the top of every bed.

Many sedimentary beds look different right-side-up and upside-down. In normal graded bedding, coarse grains sit at the bottom of a bed and fine ones at the top, so in most cases the strata get younger towards the fine side. Compression can fold beds into upside-down positions, and on an overturned wall, climbing up takes you into older beds. Reverse grading exists too, so a single bed proves nothing: geologists look for as many way-up clues as possible and check that they agree. (The wall in the reel is a sketch, not a real crag.)

Send this to the friend who thinks the top of the wall is always the youngest rock.
